title: Erling Haaland strikes late as Norway defeat Ivory Coast. But can they beat Brazil?
author: Stuart James
content:
Erling Haaland scored an 86th-minute winner as Norway beat Ivory Coast 2-1 in Dallas to set up a last 16 tie with Brazil at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on July 5.

Ivory Coast looked like they had sent the tie into extra time when Amad, on as a substitute, equalised with 74 minutes played. But Haaland, who had had a quiet game, scored with a mis-hit finish to win the match, squeezing Patrick Berg’s pass over the line.

While Ivory Coast created the better chances in an entertaining first half, it was Norway who took the lead in the 39th minute through a moment of brilliance from Antonio Nusa. The 21-year-old RB Leipzig winger dribbled into the box from the left, shuffled quickly on to his right foot and curled a superb strike into the far top corner.

Emerse Fae’s side were the better team in the second half and continued to create good chances. But Norway held out and then, with a sense of inevitability, Haaland intervened at the end.

Stuart James, Oliver Kay, Sam Lee and Liam Tharme analyse the key talking points.

For anybody new to watching Haaland… welcome to the full Erling experience.

Almost every goal he scores is a record, so here we go again: he has become the first player to score on his first three appearances at a World Cup, and the fastest player ever to score 60 international goals.

He has those 60 goals in 53 games. And yes, if you were watching most of this game wondering why he is not getting involved much, that is completely normal.

Seasoned Haaland watchers will not be surprised, of course. So far this summer he has seemed to be ultra pumped up, charging around up front, pressing defenders and goalkeepers ferociously, and scoring four in his first two games. And, while goals are basically a guarantee with the 25-year-old, that kind of energy is not always a given.

It was noticeable here that Norway were playing a conservative game, and Haaland’s own efforts seemed to be pared back, presumably an instruction by manager Stale Solbakken. The striker did what he often does: waited for the right moment to pounce. Yet, for a while, it did not seem like the moment would come at all.

Martin Odegaard, Norway's chief playmaker, was, ironically, too keen to find Haaland, but by the time he realised the pass was not on the whole chance had disappeared. In the minutes leading up to his goal, Marcus Holmgren Pedersen (twice) and Andreas Schjelderup put in poor balls Haaland had no hope of getting on the end of.

But when Oscar Bobb’s pass unlocked the Ivory Coast defence, and the ball was played across the box, of course he was there. It was not the most assured finish of Haaland's career, but it will be one of the most important: Norway can now look forward to that last-16 meeting with Brazil.

Norway’s reward for their first win in the World Cup knockout stage is a potentially daunting clash with Brazil at MetLife Stadium, New Jersey on Sunday. Remarkably, though, history is on Norway’s side.

Among the 88 teams Brazil have played in men’s international football, Norway are the only one to boast an unbeaten record against the five-time World Cup winners. True, they have only played four times, but a record of two wins and two draws — including a victory in the group stage at the 1998 World Cup — is mightily impressive; to put that in context, England have beaten Brazil just four times in 27 attempts.

Norway were not entirely convincing in overcoming Ivory Coast. But similar can be said of Brazil’s victory over Japan 24 hours earlier. We are seeing tight games settled by moments of brilliance and, while Brazil have a few potential match-winners, they do not have a goalscoring threat to match Haaland.

It will mean a chance for Haaland to renew hostilities with Gabriel, with whom he has clashed several times in the Premier League in recent seasons — notably in April, when the Arsenal and Brazil defender appeared to butt the Manchester City forward, or at least to move as if to do so. On another occasion, in September 2024, Haaland threw the ball at Gabriel while celebrating a late equaliser for City. We can expect fireworks between the pair on Sunday. Brazil will be favourites, but not overwhelmingly so.

The reaction of team-mates is always telling. Haaland stood with his arms aloft and the biggest smile you can imagine on his face. A few yards away, Odegaard held his head in his hands in a mixture of disbelief and joy. As for the rest of the Norway team, they were busy trying to catch up with the man who had just scored the goal of life.

Antonio Nusa might raise his eyebrows at that line and point out that this was merely a trademark goal for him, as it is for so many wide attackers who play inverted these days. But this is the knockout stage of the World Cup — new territory for a golden generation of Norway players.

The spotlight inevitably falls on Haaland with Norway — and for good reason; he’s a goalscoring machine. But their threat doesn’t start and end with their No 9. Nusa’s burst of pace on the left, allied to his dexterous footwork, perfectly complements a forward line that has plenty of physicality and power through Haaland and Alexander Sorloth.

All the talk before the game had been about another RB Leipzig winger – Yan Diomande. But Nusa upstaged his club team-mate here with a wonderful curling shot that arced into the top corner after he stepped inside Nicolas Pepe. Haaland was as happy as anyone to see it go in.

Stuart James

It was a tale of two substitutes who created the two goals in the second half. Amad levelled things up after a one-two on the edge of the box and a sublime dribble to find a shooting position. Fae introduced him for central midfielder Christ Inao Oulai and switched from 4-3-3 to 4-2-3-1, and it paid off. Amad combined with Pepe to break through centrally and equalise, an improvement given how wide focused Ivory Coast’s first-half attacks had been.

Just three minutes before Amad made it 1-1, Norway had made a double change, replacing Alexander Sorloth — a target-man striker at club level who plays as a wide forward internationally — with Oscar Bobb, a proper winger. Sorloth’s role for Norway is to take pressure off Haaland and receive long balls from goalkeeper Orjan Nyland. He would never play the pass that Bobb did for the winner, lock-picking the Ivory Coast defence to find Patrick Berg’s run from midfield, and he set up Haaland.

Late goals have been a theme so far in these knockouts, and both coaches using their benches continued that.

Liam Tharme
